Neonates of Parvaspina collina emerge with a shell measuring just 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] in length, a remarkably diminutive size that reflects the limited endogenous reserves available to the newly released glochidium. Following a brief period of parasitic encystment on a suitable fish host, the larva undergoes metamorphosis and settles onto the substrate. At this critical transition, the recently metamorphosed juvenile possesses a shell length of 0.03 centimeters , still barely visible to the naked eye. These early developmental stages are profoundly constrained by the energetic demands of the benthic environment, and survivorship during the first few months is typically quite low. Field surveys examining post-settlement recruitment have noted that the prodissoconch stage leaves the juvenile exceedingly vulnerable to both desiccation along fluctuating river margins and predation by benthic invertebrates. The tiny size at settlement imposes a significant bottleneck on population replenishment, as only a small fraction of the dispersed larvae encounter a microhabitat offering sufficient interstitial refuge and stable flow conditions to permit continued growth.

Laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a constant water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] have provided key insights into the early ontogeny of this species. Under these thermal conditions, the interval from ovum activation to the emergence of the free-swimming glochidium spans approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This abbreviated embryonic period is consistent with the pattern observed among other unionid bivalves that exploit a parasitic larval stage, where rapid hatching facilitates the timely encounter with a host fish. The controlled temperature regime proved essential for obtaining reproducible developmental timelines, as fluctuations in ambient thermal conditions can dramatically alter the pace of embryogenesis in freshwater mussels. Observations from these trials also confirmed that the newly hatched glochidium is entirely lecithotrophic, subsisting on the residual yolk stores that sustain it until it attaches to a host. The successful completion of the embryonic phase within this narrow thermal window is critical for synchronizing larval release with the seasonal availability of suitable fish hosts in the species' natural stream habitats.

At a rearing temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the shell length at puberty for Parvaspina collina has been recorded at 3 centimeters [Lp = 3 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for gamete production. This size threshold is attained after a protracted period of somatic growth during which the juvenile bivalve transitions from filter-feeding on phytoplankton to exploiting a broader spectrum of suspended organic particulates. Individuals at this shell length begin to develop discernible gonadal tissue, although full reproductive competence may not be achieved until a slightly larger size. The attainment of puberty at 3 cm [Lp = 3 cm] aligns this species with other slow-growing freshwater mussels inhabiting stable, low-productivity streams where energy acquisition is limiting. Comparative data from related taxa suggest that the delay in sexual maturation is an adaptive response to the uncertainty of resource availability in these environments, allowing individuals to build sufficient somatic reserves before diverting energy toward gametogenesis and spawning activities.

Adult Parvaspina collina reach a maximum recorded shell length of 7.1 centimeters [Li = 7.1 centimeters], which represents the ultimate size attained after the cessation of significant somatic growth. This asymptotic dimension is accompanied by an ultimate dry weight of 12.9 grams [Wwi = 12.9 grams], a measure that was derived from size-corrected comparisons with the closely related species Unio tumidus and reflects the substantial soft-tissue mass achieved by the oldest individuals. The shell grows slowly throughout the adult phase, with annual increments becoming progressively smaller as the animal approaches its asymptotic size. Examination of museum specimen series collected over several decades indicates that very few individuals surpass this length, suggesting a robust upper boundary to growth that is likely constrained by both genetic factors and the carrying capacity of the local habitat. The 7.1 cm [Li = 7.1 cm] shell length is somewhat smaller than that reported for several congeneric species, possibly reflecting the nutrient-poor conditions that characterize many of the streams where this mussel is endemic.

Long-term mark-recapture studies conducted at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] have documented a maximum lifespan of approximately 6,935 days [am = approximately 6,935 days] for Parvaspina collina, indicating that individuals in stable populations can survive for nearly two decades. At a shell length of 6 centimeters, reproductively active adults under these same thermal conditions have been observed to produce approximately 13,400 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 13,400 eggs per year], a single annual spawning event [F_R_i = single annual spawning event] that reflects the broad size-specific fecundity of larger females, whose spacious mantle cavities accommodate a greater number of developing ova. The extended lifespan reported here is consistent with the general life-history syndrome of freshwater mussels, which typically exhibit delayed maturity, slow growth, and high adult survival. The combination of a long reproductive window and sustained annual egg production enables populations to buffer against occasional recruitment failures, a critical demographic feature for a species inhabiting hydrologically variable stream environments.
